source.title: Provable Benefits of Overparameterization in Model Compression: From Double Descent to Pruning Neural Networks
source.authors: Xiang-Yu Chang; Ying-Cong Li; Samet Oymak; Christos Thrampoulidis

record.file_problem: Full paper text, including supplementary material, is present; some equations and figure labels are flattened, but the reported prose is readable.
record.tranche_reason: The study reports its own pruning and width experiments, refining the broad claim by showing that outcomes depend on pruning, retraining, covariance, and model setting. Its results are principally about pruning overparameterized models, rather than generalization of dense models alone.
record.gate_note: Results about natural-label generalization and random-label memorization are not tested. Results on pruning and retraining, including width sweeps, bear directly on V2. The comparisons with random pruning are included because they test whether the pruning pattern matters. Many other cited findings are background only.
record.test_reason: The study reports neural-network width sweeps with training and test errors, including dense controls, that bear on V2 in new architectures and pruning settings. Its linear-regression theory and random-feature experiments address related questions outside the listed versions.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. The authors conclude that training larger source models can improve subsequent fixed-sparsity pruning, sometimes producing double descent. Retraining benefits depend on feature correlations. Their rigorous distributional characterization concerns linear Gaussian models; random-feature equivalence and ordinary same-data retraining are supported empirically, with formal extensions left for future work.
record.recipe_differences: The listed claim versions primarily concern generalization of trained networks; this paper studies regression and neural-network pruning, typically with retraining after pruning. Neural experiments use Adam and data augmentation; theoretical analyses use least squares and Gaussian models.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcome varies with pruning method, retraining, width, sparsity target, feature covariance/correlation, and dataset/model setting. For ResNet-20, random pruning performs worse than magnitude pruning; retraining improves ResNet-20 results, while in diagonal-covariance linear models retraining can hurt except near the double-descent peak.

fits_no_version.finding: Pruned ResNet-20 test-error curves have two minima and a peak near interpolation.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Fixed-sparsity neural-network pruning can exhibit double descent as source-network width increases.

fits_no_version.finding: Linear Gaussian pruning performance depends on covariance and pruning strategy; retraining can hurt.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Overparameterized linear models can produce better sparse predictors through pruning than through direct sparse training or retraining.

fits_no_version.finding: Pruned and retrained random-feature regression attains its lowest risk with many more source features than samples.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Increasing a fixed random-feature candidate pool can improve a predictor compressed to fixed sparsity.

record.problems: Neural-network findings are presented as plots and qualitative trends without numerical test-error values in the prose. The neural experiments use data augmentation and Adam, and compare pruning procedures rather than dense-network generalization alone. The paper states that retraining theory assumes fresh samples, while ordinary retraining reuses data; the authors defer a formal analysis of that dependency.
record.rows_left_out: No additional distinct result rows were excluded; numerical risk values for some plotted linear-model curves are unavailable in the supplied text and were not inferred from figures.

untested.parts: Natural-label versus random-label fitting and held-out performance.
The original unregularized one-hidden-layer ReLU recipe, downsampled CIFAR-10, and training to demonstrated convergence. Fixed epoch counts do not establish convergence.
Matched convolutional versus fully connected comparisons and the contribution of local connectivity.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD under different tuning budgets.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and its association with generalization gaps.
Removing memorized training examples versus random examples.

missing.what: MNIST random-pruning width sweep: at low retained fractions, random pruning worsens performance, unlike magnitude pruning. Record this separately from R2.

record.verdict_notes: The study is not an original source for V2. Pruning verdicts concern an extension involving source-network width, not increasing the final sparse model's parameter count. Numerical neural-network effect sizes cannot be recovered from the supplied flattened plots.

versions.untested_parts: Natural-label versus random-label fitting and held-out accuracy.

The specified one-hidden-layer ReLU settings on MNIST and downsampled CIFAR-10 are not tested; experiments instead include pruned ResNet-20 on CIFAR-10 and two-layer fully connected networks on MNIST. The study varies width and target sparsity with pruning and retraining, not dense-network width alone.
Convolutional versus fully connected generalization and the role of local connectivity.
Adaptive optimizer versus SGD generalization comparisons.
Magnitude-aware sharpness or other measures of the generalization gap.
Removing memorized examples and measuring the effect on test accuracy.

rows.subject: ResNet-20
rows.size_stated: Width is the number of filters; target sparsities correspond to around 28,000, 70,000 and 109,000 trainable parameters.
rows.stage_stated: trained with Adam; retrained after pruning
rows.operation_detail: Trained width-k dense models, magnitude-pruned to fixed target sparsities, then retrained; measured training and test errors across width.

conditions.value: number of filters k, varying width

rows.measure: Training error and test error across width
rows.baseline: Dense width-k model; sparse models use a fixed target sparsity and are retrained.
rows.value: All curves interpolate around the same width parameter despite varying sparsity; best test error is always achieved in the overparameterized regime (large width).
rows.note: The reported result concerns pruning and retraining to fixed sparsity, not a dense model alone. The prose says training and test errors decrease as width grows except in the shaded double-descent range.
rows.check: Separate the dense width sweep from fixed-sparsity pruning results: only the dense model's final parameter count grows with width. The sparse results measure the benefit of increasing the source network's width before pruning and retraining.

rows.subject: two-layer fully connected neural network
rows.size_stated: Width is number of hidden-layer nodes; sparsity targets 4 and 8
rows.stage_stated: trained with Adam; retrained after pruning
rows.operation_detail: Trained width-k dense models, magnitude-pruned to fixed target sparsities, then retrained; measured training and test errors across width.
rows.measure: Training and test error across width
rows.baseline: Dense model and fixed-sparsity magnitude-pruned, retrained models.
rows.value: As width k grows, training and test error decrease for all dense and sparse models; training larger models benefits pruned-model accuracy; double descent is not really visible.
rows.note: The study explicitly notes no clearly visible double descent in this setting.
rows.check: The authors report decreasing test error with width for dense and magnitude-pruned, retrained models. A clearly visible double-descent peak is not required by V2. Separate dense and sparse conditions; the text does not specify the activation or establish convergence after 200 epochs.

rows.subject: ResNet-20
rows.size_stated: Width is number of filters; sparsity targets 5 and 10 filters
rows.operation_detail: Trained width-k models, randomly pruned to the same number of nonzeros as magnitude pruning, then retrained; measured test error across width.
rows.baseline: Magnitude-pruned and retrained models with the same sparsity targets.
rows.value: Double descent and downward trend are still present, but performance is worse than magnitude-based pruning.
rows.note: The text reports the comparative trend but gives no numeric values.
rows.check: Random pruning retains the downward width trend. Worse absolute performance than magnitude pruning does not make that trend partial. This concerns source-network width at fixed final sparsity.

rows.subject: ResNet-20
rows.size_stated: Width is number of filters; sparsity targets 5 and 10 filters
rows.operation_detail: Measured test error across width for magnitude-pruned models before retraining.
rows.value: Non-retrained models have much bigger test error than retrained models; overparameterization does not help in improving performance.
rows.note: This result qualifies the width benefit: it is reported for the train-prune-retrain procedure.
rows.check: The text states that increasing source-network width does not improve performance without retraining; it does not explicitly establish an opposite trend. These pruned networks are evaluated before further optimization, so this is a qualification of the pruning extension, not a counterexample to converged dense training.

source_check.correct: V2 state: cannot_determine. Non-retrained magnitude-pruned models have higher test error and no reported benefit from source overparameterization; zero training error after pruning is not established.
source_check.problem: The reported absence of a pruning benefit does not establish absence of V2's benefit after reaching zero training error.

rows.subject: ResNet-20
rows.size_stated: Width is number of filters; sparsity targets 5, 8 and 10 filters
rows.operation_detail: Measured test error across width for sparse models after magnitude pruning and retraining.
rows.value: Test error curves have two local minima; the test error peaks near the transition to zero training error.
rows.note: The double-descent peak is a reported exception to the general downward trend.
rows.check: Two minima and a peak near interpolation establish double descent, which V2 explicitly distinguishes from its claim. This row alone does not establish continued test-error reduction beyond interpolation; that evidence is already in R1.

rows.subject: Linear Gaussian problem
rows.size_stated: p features; n samples; sparsity s/p=0.1 and n/p=0.3
rows.stage_stated: least-squares ERM; pruning; some conditions retrained
rows.operation_detail: Varied the number of features k used in optimization, then applied magnitude, Hessian, or oracle pruning; measured test risk.

conditions.value: identity with spiked latent weights, or spiked diagonal covariance with identical latent weights

rows.baseline: Risk of dense ERM and risk among underparameterized solutions or retrained solutions, as shown in the figure.
rows.value: For identity covariance, magnitude and Hessian pruning coincide. With spiked covariance, Hessian pruning outperforms magnitude pruning; for Hessian and oracle pruning, the optimal sparse model is at k=p and its risk is strictly better than the minimum among underparameterized and retrained solutions.
rows.note: This concerns linear regression and pruning risk, not the V2 neural-network setting.
rows.check: Linear Gaussian regression and pruning risk do not measure any listed version's neural-network behavior.

rows.subject: random feature regression with ReLU features
rows.operation_detail: Varied p/n while pruning and retraining to fixed sparsity targets; compared empirical risks to the equivalent linear Gaussian predictions.

conditions.value: synthetic quadratic labels; input a drawn from N(0, I_d)
ReLU(Ra), R with standard normal entries
averages of 50 R realizations and 10 iterations per R

rows.baseline: Usual random feature regression with growing feature count p.
rows.value: Risks of retrained models exhibit double descent and are minimized when p is much greater than n despite fixed sparsity; theory and empirical curves exhibit a good match.
rows.note: The retraining prediction has a slight mismatch for the 4s curve; the text attributes it to reusing the same data rather than fresh retraining data.
rows.check: The input weights are fixed random features and only the output regression is fitted. This does not test V2's trained-network width claim.

rows.subject: linear Gaussian problem
rows.size_stated: rank-one covariance; n samples; sparsity s
rows.stage_stated: least-squares ERM; magnitude or Hessian pruning; retraining
rows.operation_detail: Compared expected excess population risks of pruned and retrained estimators under perfectly correlated features.
rows.value: Pruned-model excess risk is ζ²σ²/(n−2) + (1−ζ)²(λᵀβ*)²; retrained-model excess risk is σ²/(n−2).
rows.locator: Lemma 1, equations (5)–(6); Supplementary Section F, equations (97)–(98)
rows.note: This is a theoretical result about pruning and retraining, not one of the listed claim versions.
rows.check: The rank-one linear-regression risk comparison addresses pruning bias and retraining, outside the listed versions.

rows.subject: linear Gaussian problem
rows.operation_detail: Compared pruning with retraining for diagonal identity covariance and zero noise.
rows.baseline: Training a smaller regression problem on the selected features
rows.value: With all features, the larger problem recovers β* exactly; pruning can then estimate selected coefficients exactly, while solving only the smaller regression gives a noisy estimate.
rows.note: The text presents this as an intuition for a denoising effect of overparameterization.
rows.check: This is an illustrative noiseless linear-regression argument, not a neural-network width result or a separate empirical experiment.

rows.subject: linear Gaussian problem
rows.operation_detail: Derived an asymptotic distributional characterization and risk formula for magnitude pruning.

conditions.value: n,p,s grow at fixed κ=p/n>1 and α=s/p in (0,1)

rows.measure: Population risk of magnitude-pruned min-norm solution
rows.note: This is an analytic characterization, not a test of the catalog's specific natural-label generalization claim.
rows.check: An asymptotic risk characterization for pruned linear regression does not itself establish any listed version.
